subtype: Approach: separating fair feedback from abuse [Thinking]
passage: After her cooking video was shared widely, Maria sat on the sofa with her laptop and read every comment, with Nazia beside her holding tea. Maria made three piles in her head and said them aloud. 'One: valid. This person says the timings in my recipe were wrong, and they were, so I'll fix them. Two: misunderstanding. Someone thinks I used a certain oil because I was paid to, and I can say I wasn't. Three: abuse.' A handful of comments called her names and mocked her accent. 'These don't get an answer,' she said. 'Answering feeds them.' She reported the worst two to the platform and hid the rest. The first pile she answered with thanks, the second with two calm lines. It took an hour, and she felt lighter.

qa.q: How many piles did Maria sort the comments into?
qa.a: Maria sorted the comments into three piles.

qa.q: How did Maria feel after sorting and answering?
qa.a: Maria felt lighter, having put the hurtful comments aside and dealt with the useful ones.

qa.q: What other approach could Maria use next time?
qa.a: Maria could ask a trusted person to filter the comments first, so she can fix real problems without reading the abuse herself.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Maria's way of handling the comments?
qa.a: Nazia probably sees Maria staying in control and looking after herself, and may feel relieved that the hurtful comments did not swallow her.

grounding: Shows a person sorting comments into valid complaints, misunderstandings to clarify and abuse to ignore or report.

'Two hundred comments,' Kamal said, scrolling. 'Where do we even start?'
'Three piles,' Chinmay said. 'Read each one and tell me: bug, misunderstanding, or abuse.'
'"The app logs me out every time I switch screens."'
'Bug. Real. Pile one.'
'"Why do you charge for exports? It was free last year."'
'It's still free; the menu moved. Misunderstanding. Pile two, we reply and clarify.'
'"Your developers are brainless idiots, hope you go bankrupt."'
'Abuse. No reply. Pile three.'
'And this one? It has our founder's home address and "see you soon".'
Chinmay stopped. 'That's a threat. Screenshot it and report it to the platform now, and we tell the office security team today.'
By evening: thirty-one bugs logged, forty clarifications drafted, the threat reported, and a hundred-odd insults left unanswered.

qa.q: What did the comment about exports say?
qa.a: 'Why do you charge for exports? It was free last year.'

qa.q: What does Chinmay stopping at the address comment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chinmay felt alarmed, recognising a real threat that needed more than ignoring.

qa.q: Why is sorting into three piles a wise approach?
qa.a: It lets the team fix real bugs, correct misunderstandings and ignore pure abuse, instead of arguing with everyone or ignoring everything.

qa.q: How might the users who reported the logout bug see the team's approach?
qa.a: They get their problem logged and likely fixed, so they feel heard rather than lost among the insults.

grounding: It shows someone sorting comments into valid bug complaints, misunderstandings to clarify and pure abuse that gets no reply or is reported.

subtype: Approach: separating fair feedback from abuse [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Darshan, and when my cooking channel's biryani video blew up, so did the comments: six hundred of them, and some were vicious. My friend Vijay came over, and we sat with two cups of chai and a notebook.
I made myself read each comment and ask one question: is there something true here? 'The audio is too low in the second half.' True. I wrote it down. 'You didn't mention soaking time for the rice.' True, I skipped it. 'This isn't real biryani, your region doesn't even know how to cook it.' That was just a fight about regions, so no reply. And a few were pure abuse about my family. Vijay helped me report those to the platform and block the accounts.
Next week's video had better audio and a pinned note about soaking. Most of the abuse just stopped mattering to me.

qa.q: How many comments did the biryani video get?
How does Darshan feel about the abuse by the end?
qa.a: Darshan feels calmer and less hurt, since most of the abuse stopped mattering once the real feedback was separated out.

qa.q: What else could Darshan do the next time comments pour in?
qa.a: Darshan could sort them within a day using the same question and keep a list of fair points to fix in the next video.

qa.q: How might viewers who pointed out the low audio see the next video?
qa.a: They'd feel heard, seeing their fair complaint fixed without an argument.

grounding: It shows someone sorting comments into valid complaints, fights not worth answering and pure abuse to report, and fixing the fair points.
